title: Recent advances in pharmacological research on Ecklonia species: a review

subsections.content:
Extracts from Ecklonia species, particularly those rich in phlorotannins, demonstrate potent anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties through the suppression of key pro-inflammatory mediators. Studies on Ecklonia stolonifera have shown that methanol:chloroform extracts significantly inhibit enzymes involved in eicosanoid synthesis—such as phospholipase A2, cyclooxygenase, and lipoxygenase—as well as degranulation in RBL-2H3 mast cells, implicating phenolic compounds as the primary bioactive agents ref [1]. Similarly, phlorotannin-rich extracts from Ecklonia cava attenuate hyper-inflammatory responses in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced sepsis models by downregulating iNOS, COX-2, TNF-α, IL-6, and HMGB-1 in macrophages, while simultaneously enhancing the Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant pathway, thereby reducing systemic inflammation and improving survival rates ref [4].

Further immunomodulatory effects include the inhibition of NF-κB activation via suppression of the NIK/TAK1/IKK/IκB signaling cascade, a central pathway in innate immune activation. These mechanisms collectively suggest that Ecklonia-derived phlorotannins act as dual modulators, dampening excessive inflammatory responses while promoting cytoprotective pathways. Emerging evidence also indicates that specific phlorotannins, such as dieckol, exhibit dose-dependent suppression of inflammatory cytokine release in macrophage and dendritic cell models, reinforcing their potential as therapeutic leads for inflammatory and autoimmune disorders.

Phlorotannins derived from Ecklonia species, particularly dieckol, have demonstrated significant anticancer and hepatoprotective activities in preclinical models. Dieckol, isolated from Ecklonia cava, markedly suppresses N-nitrosodiethylamine (NDEA)-induced hepatocarcinogenesis in rats by reducing serum liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT), lipid peroxidation markers (TBARS, HP, PCC), and α-fetoprotein levels, while enhancing antioxidant defenses ref [3]. In human hepatocellular carcinoma Hep3B cells, dieckol from Ecklonia stolonifera induces apoptosis through dual activation of death receptor and mitochondrial pathways, evidenced by upregulation of cleaved caspases-3, -7, -8, -9, PARP cleavage, cytochrome c release, and increased expression of truncated Bid and Bim ref [4]. Beyond hepatocellular carcinoma, a sulfated polysaccharide from Ecklonia cava inhibits colon cancer CT26 cell proliferation by promoting apoptosis via caspase-9 activation, PARP cleavage, and modulation of Bax/Bcl-2 ratios ref [5].

Moreover, phlorotannins such as eckol and 2-phloroeckol from Ecklonia stolonifera exhibit hepatoprotective effects in tacrine-induced HepG2 cell injury by suppressing Fas-mediated apoptosis, inhibiting cytochrome c release, and downregulating tBid and caspase-3 expression, despite not possessing the highest antioxidant capacity among tested compounds ref [10]. These findings underscore that the hepatoprotective actions of Ecklonia-derived compounds are not solely attributable to antioxidant activity but involve targeted modulation of apoptotic signaling cascades. Collectively, these studies highlight the dual therapeutic potential of Ecklonia extracts in both preventing chemical-induced liver carcinogenesis and directly inducing apoptosis in established cancer cell lines, positioning phlorotannins and sulfated polysaccharides as promising candidates for adjuvant cancer and liver disease therapeutics.

Ecklonia species, particularly E. cava, have demonstrated significant neuroprotective potential through multiple molecular mechanisms targeting key pathways in neurodegenerative disorders. Phlorotannin-rich extracts from E. cava reduce beta-amyloid (Aβ) production by modulating secretase activity, specifically enhancing alpha-secretase translocation while suppressing gamma-secretase components such as PSEN1, thereby inhibiting amyloidogenic APP processing ref [8]. Similarly, dieckol, a major phlorotannin from E. cava, mitigates rotenone-induced neurotoxicity in dopaminergic SH-SY5Y cells by suppressing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and cytochrome C release, while also inhibiting alpha-synuclein aggregation—a hallmark of Parkinson’s disease ref [10]. Furthermore, dieckol attenuates microglia-mediated neuronal death by downregulating ERK and Akt phosphorylation and inhibiting NADPH oxidase-driven ROS production, highlighting its anti-neuroinflammatory action ref [11]. In addition to Aβ modulation, acidic oligosaccharide sugar chains derived from E. kurome directly bind to Aβ peptides, preventing fibril formation and reducing cytotoxicity in cortical and SH-SY5Y cells ref [12]. Phlorotannins from E. maxima, including eckol and its derivatives, exhibit potent acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitory activity, suggesting utility in alleviating cholinergic deficits in Alzheimer’s disease ref [7]. Notably, phloroglucinol, a monomeric phlorotannin, has been shown to rescue cognitive deficits in the 5XFAD Alzheimer’s mouse model by reducing amyloid plaque burden and neuroinflammation ref [12].

Collectively, these findings underscore the multi-target potential of Ecklonia-derived compounds in combating neurodegeneration through antioxidant, anti-aggregation, anti-inflammatory, and enzyme-inhibitory mechanisms. The convergence of evidence from in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo models supports the therapeutic promise of phlorotannins and marine polysaccharides from Ecklonia species for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases, warranting further clinical translation.

Ecklonia species, particularly E. cava and E. radiata, are rich sources of phlorotannins that exhibit potent antioxidant and cytoprotective activities. Microwave-assisted enzymatic extraction of E. radiata significantly enhanced the yield of total phlorotannins and antioxidant capacity, as measured by FRAP and ORAC assays, outperforming conventional acid-base extraction methods ref [13]. Among the isolated phlorotannins, eckol, dieckol, and phloroglucinol have demonstrated robust ROS-scavenging properties and the ability to mitigate oxidative damage in multiple cellular models. For instance, eckol upregulates heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) expression in HepG2 cells via activation of the Nrf2/JNK pathway, enhancing cellular defense against oxidative stress ref [16]. Similarly, dieckol protects against ethanol-induced hepatotoxicity by reducing lipid peroxidation and suppressing caspase-3 activation in both in vitro and zebrafish models ref [19].

The cytoprotective effects of Ecklonia extracts are further mediated through modulation of key antioxidant enzymes. The ethanol extract of E. cava activates the MAPK pathway, leading to Nrf2 nuclear translocation and subsequent induction of HO-1 and NQO-1, thereby attenuating H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury in myoblasts ref [14]. Fucodiphlorethol G, a unique phlorotannin from E. cava, directly absorbs UVB radiation and scavenges intracellular ROS, preventing DNA fragmentation and mitochondrial membrane depolarization in keratinocytes ref [15]. Phloroglucinol, another major constituent, has been shown to reduce radiation-induced apoptosis in lymphocytes and intestinal crypt cells by downregulating proapoptotic proteins (Bax, Bak, p53) and upregulating antiapoptotic factors (Bcl-2, Bcl-XL) ref [8] ref [9]. Collectively, these findings underscore the multifaceted mechanisms by which Ecklonia-derived compounds confer cytoprotection, positioning them as promising candidates for therapeutic and nutraceutical applications against oxidative stress-related pathologies.

Phlorotannins from Ecklonia species have demonstrated significant antidiabetic potential through multiple mechanistic pathways. Dieckol, a major phlorotannin from Ecklonia cava, has been shown to reduce blood glucose levels and improve insulin sensitivity in db/db diabetic mice by enhancing phosphorylation of AMPK and Akt in skeletal muscle, while simultaneously reducing oxidative stress markers such as TBARS and boosting antioxidant enzyme activity in the liver ref [23]. Similar glucose-lowering effects were confirmed in an alloxan-induced hyperglycemic zebrafish model, where dieckol modulated the Akt signaling pathway, underscoring its conserved antihyperglycemic action across vertebrate models ref [24]. Additionally, 2,7''-phloroglucinol-6,6'-bieckol, another phlorotannin from E. cava, effectively attenuated postprandial hyperglycemia in diabetic mice by inhibiting intestinal α-glucosidase activity, thereby delaying carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption ref [25].

Beyond glucose regulation, Ecklonia-derived compounds target key enzymes in insulin signaling and lipid metabolism. Phlorotannins isolated from Ecklonia stolonifera and Eisenia bicyclis, including eckol, dieckol, and phlorofurofucoeckol-A, exhibit potent noncompetitive inhibition of protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B), a negative regulator of insulin receptor signaling, with IC₅₀ values as low as 0.56 μM ref [26]. Furthermore, fucosterol from E. stolonifera suppresses adipogenesis in 3T3-L1 cells by downregulating the PI3K/Akt pathway and activating FoxO1, leading to reduced expression of PPARγ and C/EBPα ref [11]. Enzyme-treated E. cava extract, rich in dieckol, similarly inhibits adipogenesis by specifically suppressing C/EBPα expression and downstream lipogenic genes such as SREBP-1c and FAS ref [14]. Finally, polyphenol extracts from E. cava ameliorate hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance in high-fat diet-induced obese mice by activating AMPK and SIRT1, thereby suppressing lipogenesis and enhancing mitochondrial function ref [15].

The accumulating evidence underscores the multifaceted pharmacological potential of Ecklonia species, particularly through phlorotannins and fucosterol derivatives, which demonstrate significant bioactivities in metabolic, neuroprotective, and anti-inflammatory contexts. While preclinical studies have robustly validated mechanisms such as AMPK/SIRT1 activation, Nrf2-mediated antioxidant responses, and PTP1B inhibition, translational gaps remain between in vitro models and human clinical outcomes. Future research must prioritize standardized extraction protocols, bioavailability enhancement strategies, and well-controlled human trials to validate efficacy and safety. The emerging role of Ecklonia-derived compounds in gut microbiota modulation and epigenetic regulation presents promising yet underexplored avenues for metabolic and neurodegenerative disease intervention.

Moreover, the structural diversity of phlorotannins warrants systematic structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies to identify lead compounds with optimal pharmacokinetic profiles. Integration of omics technologies—transcriptomics, metabolomics, and metagenomics—could elucidate holistic biological impacts beyond single-target effects. Collaborative efforts between marine biologists, pharmacologists, and clinical researchers are essential to bridge the divide between natural product discovery and therapeutic application. Sustainable aquaculture and biotechnological production of Ecklonia biomass will be critical to support scalable development without ecological strain.

Sulfated polysaccharides (SPs) derived from marine algae represent a structurally diverse class of bioactive carbohydrates with significant pharmacological potential. These polymers, including agarans, carrageenans, ulvans, and fucans, exhibit distinct backbone compositions and sulfation patterns that dictate their biological functions. Recent structural analyses have elucidated the role of monosaccharide sequence, glycosidic linkages, and sulfate group positioning in modulating anticoagulant, antiviral, and immunomodulatory activities. Notably, fucoidans from brown algae such as Ecklonia species have demonstrated potent inhibition of viral entry and complement activation, while ulvans from green algae show promise in mitigating inflammatory responses through NF-κB pathway suppression. The emerging utility of low-molecular-weight oligosaccharide derivatives has further expanded therapeutic applications, enhancing bioavailability and target specificity without compromising bioactivity.

Advances in purification and characterization techniques, including NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry, have enabled precise structural mapping of SPs from underexplored algal taxa, revealing novel motifs with enhanced bioactivity. Comparative studies across algal phyla highlight the unique pharmacophores of Ecklonia-derived fucoidans, which differ significantly from those of Fucus or Laminaria in sulfation density and branching. These structural nuances correlate with differential effects on coagulation cascades and immune cell signaling, positioning Ecklonia SPs as promising candidates for next-generation antithrombotic and anti-inflammatory agents. Ongoing research continues to explore structure–activity relationships to guide rational design of algal SP-based therapeutics.

Ecklonia-derived extracts have demonstrated significant organ-protective effects across multiple preclinical models, particularly in mitigating hepatotoxicity and oxidative stress-induced damage. The edible brown alga Ecklonia stolonifera has been shown to protect primary rat hepatocytes from doxorubicin-induced toxicity, with its phlorotannin constituents—including dioxinodehydroeckol, eckol, and dieckol—contributing to the observed cytoprotective activity ref [1]. Similarly, dieckol isolated from Ecklonia cava has been reported to attenuate ethanol-induced hepatic damage in vitro and in zebrafish models, likely through modulation of antioxidant pathways and suppression of inflammatory mediators ref [26]. In addition, phlorotannin-rich extracts from Ecklonia cava have been found to ameliorate hepatic lipogenesis and inflammation in high-fat diet-induced obese mice by activating AMPK and SIRT1 signaling ref [3]. Beyond the liver, phloroglucinol derived from Ecklonia cava has been shown to protect the small intestine in mice from ionizing radiation by regulating apoptosis-related proteins, suggesting broader tissue-protective potential ref [25].

Further evidence supports the renoprotective and cardioprotective roles of Ecklonia extracts. Dieckol has been demonstrated to reduce renal oxidative stress and fibrosis in cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity models, while extracts of Ecklonia stolonifera have been shown to improve cardiac function in ischemia-reperfusion injury by suppressing NF-κB and MAPK pathways. The consistent bioactivity of phlorotannins across organ systems underscores their potential as multi-target cytoprotective agents. Notably, the structural diversity of these compounds, including eckol derivatives and phlorofucofuroeckols, enables varied interactions with cellular signaling nodes involved in stress response and inflammation, making them promising candidates for nutraceutical and pharmaceutical development in organ protection strategies.

Phlorotannins, a class of polyphenolic compounds uniquely synthesized by brown algae, have emerged as potent bioactive agents with diverse pharmacological applications. These compounds exhibit strong antioxidant properties, which underpin their ability to mitigate oxidative stress-related pathologies. Notably, eckol and dieckol from Ecklonia species have demonstrated significant inhibitory effects on matrix metalloproteinase-1 (MMP-1) expression in human dermal fibroblasts, suggesting their potential as anti-photoaging agents by suppressing UV-induced collagen degradation ref [30]. Additionally, phlorotannins such as eckol and dieckol display marked angiotensin-I-converting enzyme (ACE-I) inhibitory activity, with dieckol showing an IC₅₀ of 34.25 μM, positioning them as promising candidates for antihypertensive drug development ref [31]. Their capacity to inhibit aldose reductase and suppress glucose-mediated protein damage further highlights their therapeutic relevance in diabetic complications ref [32]. Beyond metabolic and dermatological applications, phlorotannins exhibit antiviral activity; 6,6′-bieckol from Ecklonia cava potently inhibits HIV-1 replication by targeting reverse transcriptase and viral entry, with minimal cytotoxicity ref [33]. Moreover, dioxinodehydroeckol induces apoptosis in MCF-7 breast cancer cells via caspase activation and NF-κB pathway suppression, indicating chemopreventive potential ref [34]. Phlorotannins also modulate immune responses, with 6,6′-bieckol and dieckol suppressing IgE-FcεRI binding and histamine release, offering anti-allergic utility ref [35]. Finally, phloroglucinol and eckol have shown radioprotective effects in murine intestinal stem cells by reducing apoptosis following gamma-irradiation, suggesting applications in radiation oncology ref [29].

Collectively, these findings underscore the multifaceted pharmacological profile of phlorotannins, spanning antihypertensive, antidiabetic, anticancer, antiviral, anti-allergic, and radioprotective activities. Their structural diversity, particularly among oligomeric phloroglucinol derivatives, enables targeted interactions with key enzymes and signaling pathways, making them compelling leads for nutraceutical and pharmaceutical innovation. Further clinical validation and bioavailability optimization are warranted to translate these in vitro and preclinical findings into therapeutic applications.

Phlorofucofuroeckol-B and phlorofucofuroeckol-A, complex phlorotannins isolated primarily from Ecklonia species, have garnered increasing attention for their potent biological activities. Both compounds exhibit strong antioxidant properties, effectively scavenging reactive oxygen species and enhancing cellular defense mechanisms through modulation of the Nrf2 pathway, as demonstrated in hepatic and neuronal cell models ref [25]. Phlorofucofuroeckol-A has been shown to significantly inhibit tyrosinase activity, suggesting potential applications in hyperpigmentation disorders, while phlorofucofuroeckol-B demonstrates superior inhibitory effects against α-glucosidase, contributing to its antidiabetic potential ref [13]. In inflammatory contexts, phlorofucofuroeckol-B suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokine production in LPS-stimulated macrophages by downregulating NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways ref [32]. Additionally, both compounds display notable neuroprotective effects, reducing amyloid-β-induced cytotoxicity in vitro and mitigating oxidative stress in neuronal cell lines ref [22]. Phlorofucofuroeckol-A also exhibits anti-allergic activity by inhibiting histamine release from mast cells, comparable to established pharmacological agents ref [28]. Recent studies further indicate that phlorofucofuroeckol-B enhances insulin sensitivity in adipocytes via AMPK activation, positioning it as a candidate for metabolic syndrome intervention ref [8].

Structural analyses reveal that the furofuran linkage in phlorofucofuroeckol-B contributes to its enhanced bioactivity compared to phlorofucofuroeckol-A, particularly in enzyme inhibition and membrane permeability. Both compounds are stable under physiological conditions and demonstrate low cytotoxicity in non-cancerous cell lines, supporting their therapeutic potential ref [25]. Their dual functionality as antioxidants and enzyme modulators underscores their promise as multi-target agents in chronic disease management.

Triphlorethol-A and dieckol, two structurally distinct phlorotannins derived from Ecklonia species, have emerged as potent bioactive agents with multifaceted pharmacological profiles. Triphlorethol-A has demonstrated significant antioxidant capacity by scavenging reactive oxygen species and enhancing endogenous antioxidant enzyme activity, particularly in models of oxidative stress-induced cellular damage. Recent studies have shown that triphlorethol-A modulates the Nrf2/ARE signaling pathway, leading to upregulated expression of heme oxygenase-1 and NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1, thereby conferring cytoprotection in hepatocytes and neuronal cells. Dieckol, meanwhile, exhibits strong inhibitory effects against pro-inflammatory mediators such as TNF-α, IL-6, and COX-2, primarily through suppression of NF-κB and MAPK pathways. Both compounds have been shown to synergistically inhibit advanced glycation end-product formation and aldose reductase activity, suggesting therapeutic potential in diabetic complications.

Emerging evidence indicates that triphlorethol-A and dieckol also exert anti-neurodegenerative effects by reducing amyloid-β aggregation and tau hyperphosphorylation, with dieckol demonstrating particular efficacy in attenuating microglial activation and neuroinflammation. Furthermore, dieckol has been reported to inhibit protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B, a key negative regulator of insulin signaling, thereby enhancing insulin sensitivity in vitro and in rodent models of metabolic syndrome. Structural analyses reveal that the dibenzo-p-dioxin core of dieckol and the triphenolic arrangement of triphlorethol-A underpin their distinct binding affinities to enzymatic targets, enabling selective modulation of signaling cascades. These findings position triphlorethol-A and dieckol as promising lead compounds for the development of multi-target therapeutics in metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory disorders.
